results.title: When even your Traffic Fine is a scam!
results.content: Once upon a time in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, the government decided that Ghanaian motorists had enjoyed too much freedom on the roads. Some drove as though speed limits were recommendations from elderly relatives, deserving respectful consideration but not necessarily obedience. Others regarded traffic lights as Christmas decorations, beautiful to behold but entirely optional. The authorities therefore introduced electronic traffic enforcement, hoping cameras would accomplish what policemen, road signs and decades of public education had struggled to achieve. It was a brilliant idea. Cameras do not accept apologies, recognise party colours or appreciate the significance of a driver's uncle being a Deputy Minister. They simply record offences and leave the authorities to do the rest.

results.title: Ghana’s new export miracle: From Cocoa to Cocaine!
results.content: Once upon a time in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, a country famous for producing cocoa, gold and excellent excuses discovered that its agricultural export industry had acquired a rather mysterious new product. The discovery was not made at the Ministry of Trade, the Ghana Export Promotion Authority or any of those important conferences where distinguished gentlemen gather to discuss value addition over bottled water and meat pies. It was made in Spain, where customs officers opened a consignment of Ghanaian coconuts and discovered that the fruits had apparently travelled with 2.6 tonnes of cocaine. The call was made at just ended Local Content Conference and Exhibition (LCCE), where industry stakeholders stressed that building a resilient, competitive and sustainable oil and gas sector requires more than policies promoting indigenous participation.
